Educational neuroscience

Words: 86 Articles: 2
Neuroscience OurBigBook.com
Research connecting neural processes with questions about learning and education. A plausible neural mechanism is not sufficient evidence that a particular classroom method improves pupil outcomes.

Neuromyth

Words: 31
Educational neuroscience OurBigBook.com
A misconception presented as a consequence of brain knowledge or used as a brain-based educational explanation. Not every unsupported educational claim is specifically neuroscientific, so survey categories and definitions need examination.

Neuroscience literacy

Words: 30
Educational neuroscience OurBigBook.com
Understanding relevant brain science and how to evaluate claims derived from it. Knowing isolated facts should be distinguished from reasoning about a new educational claim and selecting an effective intervention.

Neurodiversity

Words: 25
Neuroscience OurBigBook.com
Variation in neurological and cognitive characteristics across people. Describing variation does not settle which features cause disability or which forms of support an individual needs.

Motor control

Words: 85 Articles: 2
Neuroscience OurBigBook.com
Processes that plan, initiate and adjust movement using internal goals and sensory information. A deficit in execution can mimic poor motor learning unless baseline performance and improvement with practice are assessed separately.

Spatial stimulus-response compatibility

Words: 25
Motor control OurBigBook.com
Facilitation or interference caused by correspondence between stimulus location and response location. It can mimic an imitation effect if location and action identity are not separated.

Motor simulation

Words: 30
Motor control OurBigBook.com
Use of representations related to one’s own action system while processing another action. Evidence for recruitment must be distinguished from evidence that simulation is necessary for every form of understanding.

Lateralization of brain function

Words: 95 Articles: 1
Neuroscience OurBigBook.com
A functional asymmetry between cerebral hemispheres, measured for a stated task, contrast or operation. Population-level left dominance does not imply complete right-side inactivity or an identical pattern in every individual.

Laterality index (LI=(L−R)/(L+R))

Words: 66
Lateralization of brain function OurBigBook.com
For nonnegative measurements L,R with L+R>0, one convention is LI=(L−R)/(L+R). The bound ∣L−R∣≤L+R gives −1≤LI≤1. Multiplying both measurements by the same positive factor leaves the index unchanged. A change from (L,R)=(20,10) to (10,10) changes the index from 1/3 to 0 without increasing R. Thus a reduced leftward index alone cannot establish right-side recruitment. Baseline, threshold and negative-response conventions must be specified.

Chemogenetics

Words: 62 Articles: 1
Neuroscience OurBigBook.com
Perturbing cellular function using a pharmacologically responsive introduced component. Ligand metabolism and actions on endogenous receptors require controls; genetic targeting alone does not guarantee a specific behavioural mechanism.

DREADD

Words: 35
Chemogenetics OurBigBook.com
Designer receptors used to alter cell signalling in response to an administered ligand. The name does not establish that the ligand is inert elsewhere or that its administered form is the species acting in the brain.

Acoustic startle reflex

Words: 27
Neuroscience OurBigBook.com
A rapid response to an abrupt sound. Its amplitude can be modulated by threat, attention, motor capacity and drugs; baseline startle and potentiation should be examined separately.

Opioidergic modulation

Words: 33
Neuroscience OurBigBook.com
Regulation through opioid-receptor signaling. Blocking such signaling can test its causal contribution to a task response, but a system-level pharmacological effect does not identify the same neurons as the representation of two different experiences.

Neuroplasticity

Words: 164 Articles: 4
Neuroscience OurBigBook.com
Changes in the functional organization, connectivity or physiological operation of neural systems with experience, altered input or development. Rapid unmasking and slower structural reorganization are different candidate mechanisms; an imaging activation change alone does not distinguish them.

Maladaptive plasticity

Words: 29
Neuroplasticity OurBigBook.com
A change in neural organisation that worsens or constrains function under specified conditions. Increased activation alone does not establish maladaptation; a controlled intervention must test the proposed harmful contribution.

Functional compensation

Words: 29
Neuroplasticity OurBigBook.com
A contribution from an altered or additionally recruited system that supports performance after disruption. Compensation can be necessary yet incomplete, and can differ across regions, tasks and recovery stages.

Crossmodal plasticity

Words: 69 Articles: 1
Neuroplasticity OurBigBook.com
Changes in the contribution of one sensory system to processing information from another modality, often investigated after altered sensory input. Imaging can identify recruitment; causal perturbation can test whether the recruited network contributes to a task.

Sensory compensation

Words: 33
Crossmodal plasticity OurBigBook.com
Adaptation supporting task performance when sensory input is reduced. Practice, altered attention, use of alternative cues and changes in neural recruitment can interact. Improvement in one task can coexist with limitations in another.

Behavioural neuroscience

Words: 16
Neuroscience OurBigBook.com
Study of the biological mechanisms of behaviour and cognition, using converging behavioural, physiological and intervention evidence.

Neuroscientific methods

Words: 316 Articles: 8
Neuroscience OurBigBook.com
Methods for measuring and manipulating nervous-system structure and function. The inference permitted by a recording, an anatomical reconstruction and a perturbation differs; convergence is more informative than treating them as interchangeable.

Functional localizer

Words: 38
Neuroscientific methods OurBigBook.com
An independently specified task contrast used to identify a region for subsequent analysis. Individual localisation can distinguish neighbouring language-selective and domain-general regions, while independent data reduce circularity.[ref]

Structural connectivity

Words: 26
Neuroscientific methods OurBigBook.com
Anatomical links among neural regions. Diffusion-based tractography estimates aspects of white-matter organisation indirectly and should not be equated with a direct count of synapses or information flow.

Functional connectivity

Words: 25
Neuroscientific methods OurBigBook.com
Statistical dependence between activity measurements from different locations. Resting-state correlation does not establish direct anatomical connectivity, the direction of influence or a causal role in behaviour.

Voxel

Words: 33
Neuroscientific methods OurBigBook.com
A volume element in an imaging measurement. In functional magnetic resonance imaging, one voxel aggregates an indirect signal over many cells, so a shared response at voxel or region scale need not imply the same active neuronal population.

Single-unit recording

Words: 41
Neuroscientific methods OurBigBook.com
Measurement of the activity attributed to one neuron, commonly through extracellular electrodes and spike isolation. It permits trial-resolved tests of stimulus tuning and interactions. Failure to evoke spikes with one stimulus alone does not exclude a modulatory input from that modality.

Lesion study

Words: 47
Neuroscientific methods OurBigBook.com
A study relating damage to altered or preserved performance. Damage may affect several neighboring areas and connections, and chronic compensation can change the relationship between a lesion and behavior. Deficits are evidence about a network's contribution under the tested conditions, not automatic localization of one abstract faculty.

Transcranial magnetic stimulation

Words: 75 Articles: 1
Neuroscientific methods OurBigBook.com
Noninvasive stimulation in which a changing magnetic field induces electrical effects in neural tissue. Task-specific perturbation and control conditions can test causal hypotheses, but stimulation can affect connected regions and does not isolate a unique cellular mechanism.

Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation

Words: 38
Transcranial magnetic stimulation OurBigBook.com
Repeated magnetic stimulation used to perturb cortical activity or investigate changes after a stimulation intervention. The physiological effect and network spread depend on site, state and protocol; a nominally inhibitory manipulation does not guarantee a purely local reduction.

Cognitive neuroscience

Words: 1k Articles: 44
Neuroscience OurBigBook.com
The study of neural mechanisms underlying cognition, using converging behavioral, physiological, imaging, computational and intervention evidence. A location associated with a task is not by itself an explanation of the task's computation.

Cognitive reserve

Words: 30
Cognitive neuroscience OurBigBook.com
Resources or strategies allowing performance to remain effective despite brain changes. A later clinical symptom onset can be compatible with reserve without implying a lower disease incidence or less underlying pathology.

Body representation

Words: 73 Articles: 2
Cognitive neuroscience OurBigBook.com
Representations of the body used for sensation, action and judgments about body parts or ownership. These functions can dissociate, so the term need not denote one unified map.

Somatoparaphrenia

Words: 26
Body representation OurBigBook.com
A disturbed belief about ownership of a body part, for example attributing one’s limb to another person. This goes beyond inaccurate localization of a visual target.

Asomatognosia

Words: 19
Body representation OurBigBook.com
Impaired acknowledgment or recognition of part of one’s body. It is not interchangeable with every form of visual neglect.

Neural representation

Words: 203 Articles: 4
Cognitive neuroscience OurBigBook.com
A pattern of neural activity that carries task-relevant information under a specified decoding or explanatory model. Anatomical co-location, similar mean activation and a shared representational code are different claims.

Amodal representation

Words: 68 Articles: 1
Neural representation OurBigBook.com
A representation whose relevant information is independent of a particular sensory or output modality. Shared mean activation across modalities is weaker evidence than generalisation of information about the represented content, with confounded stimuli and responses controlled.
Amodal semantics
Words: 32
Amodal representation OurBigBook.com
Conceptual information accessible through different forms such as words, signs and pictures. Shared conceptual content can coexist with modality-specific input and output pathways; an anatomical overlap alone does not establish identical neural codes.

Regional activation does not identify a neural code

Words: 71
Neural representation OurBigBook.com
Consider two response vectors x=(3,1,3,1) and y=(3,3,1,1) over the same four measured locations, relative to a zero baseline. Both are positive everywhere and have mean two. Their centered vectors xc​=(1,−1,1,−1) and yc​=(1,1,−1,−1) satisfy xc​⋅yc​=0. Hence identical positive regional means can accompany orthogonal patterns. This counterexample shows why overlapping regional activation does not imply a shared neural representation. It does not assert that real neural codes are necessarily orthogonal or that unsuccessful decoding proves their independence.

Neural code

Words: 36
Neural representation OurBigBook.com
The relationship between a neural activity pattern and information represented by that pattern. Testing a shared neural code requires more than activation in the same anatomical territory: the informative pattern or mapping must generalize under an appropriate comparison.

Language processing

Words: 902 Articles: 33
Cognitive neuroscience OurBigBook.com
Processes supporting language comprehension and production. Neural models must distinguish the transformations required by a task from correlated memory, decision and motor demands.

Literacy-related cortical reorganisation

Words: 35
Language processing OurBigBook.com
Differences in neural responses associated with literacy experience. Comparisons including adult learners constrain purely childhood explanations while remaining vulnerable to nonrandom educational histories.[ref]

Word recognition

Words: 238 Articles: 7
Language processing OurBigBook.com
Identification of a word form under a specified input modality. Accuracy, speed and access to meaning are distinguishable measurements.
Word frequency
Words: 22
Word recognition OurBigBook.com
How often a word occurs in a defined language sample or learning history. Corpus frequency and an individual child's actual exposure need not coincide.
Visual word recognition
Words: 197 Articles: 5
Word recognition OurBigBook.com
Identification of printed word forms. Familiar-word accuracy, unfamiliar-word decoding, fluent access and semantic interpretation should not be treated as interchangeable outcomes.
Orthographic learning
Words: 153 Articles: 3
Visual word recognition OurBigBook.com
Acquisition of information about written forms and their relations. Retention of a particular spelling and generalisation to untrained combinations are different outcomes.
Variability in irrelevant letters
Words: 46
Orthographic learning OurBigBook.com
Variation in surrounding letters while a target mapping remains stable. A first-grade training experiment found transfer benefits from varied consonants around vowel mappings, motivating tests of how example distributions support abstraction.[ref]
Artificial-orthography learning experiment
Words: 47
Orthographic learning OurBigBook.com
Participants learn controlled written forms, pronunciations and sometimes meanings, followed by trained-item and transfer tests. Manipulating frequency and consistency can test sensitivity to input structure without uniquely identifying a learning algorithm.[ref]
Self-teaching hypothesis of reading
Words: 39
Orthographic learning OurBigBook.com
The proposal that phonological recoding of unfamiliar written forms creates opportunities to acquire word-specific orthographic representations. Delayed discrimination from homophonic alternatives tests more than immediate pronunciation.[ref]

Consider two equally weighted sets of event triples: {(A,L,1),(B,R,2)} and {(A,R,1),(B,L,2)}. Their separate distributions of item, place and time are identical, but P(L∣A) is respectively 1 and 0. Words: 103 Articles: 1
Multisensory integration OurBigBook.com
Inference about whether sensory signals have a common source or separate sources. Bayes' theorem compares hypotheses through P(C∣x)∝P(x∣C)P(C). A common-source hypothesis can permit cue combination; separate-source hypotheses can preserve distinct estimates. Reliability weighting conditional on a common source is therefore not the entire causal-inference problem.

Words: 56

For a common-event model, let y∣δ∼N(δ,s2) and δ∼N(0,τ2) with positive variances. The posterior exponent is −[(y−δ)2/s2+δ2/τ2]/2. Completing the square yields posterior precision s−2+τ−2 and mean yτ2/(s2+τ2). The estimate is pulled toward zero, more strongly when the measurement is uncertain. This conditional model does not decide whether a common event should be assumed.

Words: 115 Articles: 1
Multisensory cue integration OurBigBook.com
A cue-combination rule weighting more precise estimates more strongly. For independent unbiased Gaussian estimates of one quantity and a flat prior, inverse-variance weights are both minimum-variance linear and maximum-likelihood weights. The assumptions exclude arbitrary averaging of complementary qualities such as odor identity and gustatory sweetness.
Minimum-variance two-cue estimate (w1​=σ22​/(σ12​+σ22​))
Words: 70
Reliability-weighted cue integration OurBigBook.com
Let unbiased independent estimates X1​,X2​ have variances a,b>0. The variance of wX1​+(1−w)X2​ is w2a+(1−w)2b. Its derivative is 2w(a+b)−2b and its second derivative is 2(a+b)>0, proving the unique optimum w=b/(a+b) and variance ab/(a+b). Independent Gaussian likelihoods give the same estimate by differentiating (x1​−x)2/a+(x2​−x)2/b. With covariance c, the variance becomes w2a+(1−w)2b+2w(1−w)c, and the unconstrained optimum is (b−c)/(a+b−2c) when the denominator is positive; it need not lie between zero and one.

Voltage clamp

Neuroscience OurBigBook.com
A voltage clamp uses electrical feedback to hold a preparation's membrane potential near a commanded value while measuring the electric current required to maintain it. Holding voltage separates changes in electrical conductance from changes in electrical driving force. Imperfect voltage control and finite recording bandwidth limit the inference. The muscle experiment under ionotropic receptor used separate intracellular electrodes for voltage control and a sealed patch pipette for recording local electric current.[ref]

Extracellular single-unit recording

Neuroscience OurBigBook.com

Primary visual cortex (V1)

Words: 2k Articles: 12
Neuroscience OurBigBook.com
The primary visual cortex, often abbreviated V1, is an early cortical stage of visual processing. Its neurons have receptive fields: changing a stimulus in a particular part of the visible scene can change their spike trains. Orientation selectivity adds a further distinction: at the same location, a properly aligned bar can evoke a strong response while a rotated bar evokes little. Simple cells make the dependence on local position and visual contrast especially clear. See the original experiments under orientation selectivity and simple cell.
In their 1962 study, David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel recorded from forty cats under thiopental anesthesia, maintained light anesthesia while monitoring cortical electrical activity, and used succinylcholine to stabilize the eyes. White-light patterns were projected onto a screen 1.5m away. Extracellular single-unit recording with tungsten electrodes sampled individual units; receptive fields were mapped separately for each eye. This connected controlled stimulus geometry to individual spike trains. [ref]
These acute, anesthetized-cat recordings do not directly measure human perception or responses during awake behavior. The useful idea is a local description of structure: a population can distinguish where a feature lies, which way it is aligned, and which side is brighter. The signed spatial filter model of a simple cell turns that idea into a computable example. One neuron's preferred stimulus does not establish recognition of an entire object. Likewise, orientation selectivity in one neuron and an orderly map of preferences across primary visual cortex are different findings: rodents can have strong orientation selectivity without the orderly arrangement typical of some other species. [ref] The existing correlation-based development of visual cortical maps and orientation-map self-organization sections describe hypotheses about how organization develops.

It cancels a spatially uniform opponent signal but responds when the regions differ. Such filtering can support chromatic boundaries without by itself solving every illumination ambiguity.

Correlation-based development of visual cortical maps

Words: 61
Primary visual cortex OurBigBook.com
Consider afferent activities zi​, cortical activity ya​ and a constrained Hebbian learning rule w˙ai​=ϵ⟨ya​zi​⟩−Λa​. If ya​=∑b,j​Kab​wbj​zj​, then ⟨ya​zi​⟩=∑b,j​Kab​wbj​Cji​, where C is the input correlation matrix. Thus input correlations and lateral interactions select growing weight modes, while synaptic normalization and bounds stop unlimited growth. The model tests how organization can emerge without assigning every final cortical feature in advance.

Complex cell

Words: 169 Articles: 2
Primary visual cortex OurBigBook.com
A complex cell typically responds selectively to an oriented edge or bar over a finite spatial region with less dependence on spatial phase and contrast polarity than a simple cell. It need not have the simple cell's separated linear ON and OFF subregions. Phase tolerance is local, not invariance to arbitrary displacement outside its receptive field.

Quadrature energy model of a complex cell (E=(ke​∗I)2+(ko​∗I)2)

Complex cell OurBigBook.com
Two oriented linear filters in quadrature have responses Acosφ and Asinφ to a suitably matched narrowband grating. Their squared sum is A2, independent of phase φ, while orientation and spatial-frequency selectivity remain. A nonlinear output function or normalization can transform this energy into firing rate. Ideal quadrature gives an exact phase identity for the matched stimulus; finite approximate filter pairs need not have perfect invariance for arbitrary images.

Pooling model of a complex cell

Complex cell OurBigBook.com
Rectify outputs of simple cells with similar orientations and varying phases or positions, then sum or pool them. Opposite-polarity subunits allow response to both light and dark features. Pooling gives approximate phase and position tolerance over the subunit coverage; its extent and contrast dependence depend on the pooling rule.

Activity-dependent ocular dominance segregation

Ocular dominance column OurBigBook.com
Two eye-specific afferent populations compete under Hebbian learning and synaptic normalization. In a simplified symmetric two-eye model, the eye-difference mode da​=waL​−waR​ evolves with a linear operator containing Kab​(Csame​−Ccross​)ab​. Dominant spatial modes can produce alternating eye preference, while saturation sets finite contrast. The interaction width, arbor constraints and correlation structure influence the column scale. This is a mechanistic hypothesis whose predictions can be tested, not a unique inference from the existence of columns.

Orientation selectivity

Words: 532 Articles: 2
Primary visual cortex OurBigBook.com
Orientation selectivity is a systematic dependence of a visual neuron's response on the axis of a bar, edge or stripe pattern presented in its receptive field, under specified stimulus conditions. Here the angle θ measures the stripe axis from horizontal: 0∘ is horizontal and 90∘ vertical. An axis has no arrow, so θ and θ+180∘ describe the same orientation. A preference for one direction of movement across that axis is an additional property; the 1962 recordings included both equal and unequal responses to opposite movements. [ref]
A particularly clear experiment using extracellular single-unit recording appears in the 1959 paper, Figures 2–3. A bright 1∘×8∘ slit was centered on the same receptive field and rotated through successive angles; each presentation lasted one second. The vertical slit strongly increased the extracellularly recorded spike train, whereas the horizontal slit was ineffective. Small-spot tests had identified ON and OFF receptive-field subregions, with a central ON region and opposing flanks: rotation illuminated less of the center and more of the flanks. Geometry and location therefore mattered together. These dimensions belong to that recorded unit, not to every neuron. [ref]
An orientation tuning curve summarizes a controlled angle sweep. Keep location, size and visual contrast fixed; for a stripe pattern also specify spatial frequency and phase. The same signed spatial filter model of a simple cell can produce strong orientation selectivity and strong dependence on phase, as the following original toy illustrates. Its smooth curves are calculated predictions, not digitized or invented biological measurements.

Orientation tuning curve (r(θ))

Words: 162
Orientation selectivity OurBigBook.com
An orientation tuning curve plots a specified response against the stimulus-axis angle θ, with the other stimulus variables controlled. A practical count summary for extracellular single-unit recording is
r(θ)=mT1​∑k=1m​Nk​(θ),
(1)
where Nk​(θ) counts action potentials in the same duration T>0 on trial k, and m is the number of repeats at each angle. This estimates spikes per unit time in that window; the window must specify whether it covers onset, sustained stimulation, or both. Record a blank-background response separately, and report whether it has been subtracted. Randomizing angle order and repeating each condition helps separate orientation selectivity from changes over time, including neural adaptation. This is a proposed measurement procedure, not a claim that the original experiments used this estimator.
A simple cell's orientation tuning curve can also change when the stimulus shifts. An angle sweep at fixed phase, a sweep averaging over phase, and a sweep of moving stripes ask different questions. Consequently, a single preferred angle does not specify the whole receptive field. The toy curve under orientation selectivity holds phase fixed and plots dimensionless output, rather than spikes per second.

Orientation-map self-organization

Words: 52
Orientation selectivity OurBigBook.com
Correlation-based learning among spatially arranged ON and OFF inputs, with synaptic competition and lateral interactions, can select elongated simple cell receptive fields. Neighbor interactions coordinate preferred orientations across cortex, while competition allows different orientations to persist. Selectivity within one cell and a spatial map across many cells are separate predictions, and neither follows from unbounded Hebbian learning alone.

Simple cell

Words: 716 Articles: 1
Primary visual cortex OurBigBook.com
A simple cell is a visual cortical neuron whose receptive field has spatially separable ON and OFF receptive-field subregions. Elongated neighboring subregions give a preferred orientation and a sensitivity to the location and polarity of visual contrast. “Simple” describes the response organization; it does not describe a simpler cell body or a particular shape of neuron.
Hubel and Wiesel's 1962 classification emphasized four observations: distinguishable ON and OFF receptive-field subregions, summation within each region, antagonism between regions, and qualitative prediction of responses to differently shaped stimuli from those regions' arrangement. A slit fitting an elongated center was more effective than a smaller spot; a larger patch could invade opposing flanks and lose effectiveness. An edge separating bright and dark regions could be effective when its boundary matched the boundary between subregions. These were observations about spike trains, rather than an assertion of exact linearity. [ref]
The following deliberately coarse signed spatial filter model of a simple cell makes the geometry easy to count. A centered bright bar contributes positively at five sites. Rotating it preserves its area but mixes positive and negative weights; shifting it preserves its orientation but changes which weights it samples. The model is useful because it predicts distinct effects of these three manipulations instead of treating any bright stimulus as equivalent.
A simple cell is not an ideal linear sensor. Its spike train is nonnegative in event count, and neural adaptation can change responsiveness. The signed spatial filter model of a simple cell supplies a useful approximation to spatial drive and an explicit output rule. Comparing predictions with unseen stimuli is more informative than assuming the rule from the name “simple”. In contrast, the existing complex cell models explore tolerance to phase and local displacement.

Signed spatial filter model of a simple cell (D=∑i,j​Kij​Cij​,R=max(0,D))

Words: 388
Simple cell OurBigBook.com
A signed spatial filter model of a simple cell assigns a weight Kij​ to each sampled location and takes its dot product with the visual contrast image Cij​. Positive weights favor bright features; negative weights favor dark features. The signed drive
D=∑i,j​Kij​Cij​,R=max(0,D)
(2)
is a linear function of the image, while the rectified linear unit output R is nonlinear. D and R below are arbitrary model units. To obtain a predicted firing rate one would need a calibrated gain, background response and possibly a different output function. The model does not generate a spike train; a linear-nonlinear-Poisson cascade model adds a stochastic event-generation assumption.
For the first diagram, every one of five rows has weights
(Ki1​,Ki2​,Ki3​,Ki4​,Ki5​)=(−1/20,−1/20,1/5,−1/20,−1/20).
(3)
A bright central column, with Ci3​=1 and zero elsewhere, gives D=5/5=1. A bright middle row gives D=−1/20−1/20+1/5−1/20−1/20=0; a uniformly bright patch also gives D=0, since every row sums to zero. Move the bright column one site right: D=5(−1/20)=−1/4, so R=0. Make that shifted column dark instead: D=1/4 and R=1/4. Thus an OFF-like weight can increase output for darkness. A negative weight is a descriptive sensitivity, not evidence for a particular inhibitory synapse.
For a smooth example use the real, even Gabor filter
K(x,y)=exp(−2σx2​x2​−2σy2​y2​)cos(qx),Cθ,φ​(x,y)=cos(q(xsinθ−ycosθ)+φ).
(4)
The Gaussian function localizes the weights; the cosine supplies alternating polarity. Choose σx​=1/2, σy​=1 and q=π in arbitrary spatial units. The stripes' spatial frequency is q/(2π)=1/2 cycles per unit. Their axis makes angle θ with horizontal, while brightness changes across the perpendicular axis. φ is their spatial phase. Normalize the full-plane integral of KCθ,φ​ by its value at θ=π/2, φ=0. The Gaussian integral and the product identity for cosines give
D(θ,φ)=A(θ)cosφ,R(θ,φ)=max(0,D(θ,φ)),
(5)
where
A(θ)=1+exp(−2σx2​q2)exp[−2q2​(σx2​(sinθ−1)2+σy2​cos2θ)]+exp[−2q2​(σx2​(sinθ+1)2+σy2​cos2θ)]​.
(6)
At φ=0, horizontal stripes give R≈0.004159, 60∘ stripes give R≈0.286741, and vertical stripes give R=1. At the same vertical orientation, φ=π/2 gives D=R=0, while reversing the polarity with φ=π gives D=−1 and R=0. The preferred axis persists while the response changes dramatically with position. Shifting the vertical stripes by a quarter of their wavelength changes phase by π/2 up to sign, without rotating them.
These are two different toy filters, not discretizations of the same fitted receptive field. The discrete filter exactly rejects a uniform contrast patch; this Gabor filter need not reject uniform contrast because its weight integral need not vanish. Neither toy includes stimulus history, recurrent interactions, saturation or a measured response baseline. Their value is a transparent prediction: orientation selectivity can emerge from spatial summation, and it does not by itself imply tolerance to phase.

Patch clamp

Words: 2k Articles: 17
Neuroscience OurBigBook.com
Patch clamp connects an electrode to a small area of cell membrane through a solution-filled patch pipette. A gigaohm seal around the rim makes tiny electric currents through ion channels distinguishable from seal leak current. The beautiful change of scale is from a population's average response to individual opening and closing events in single-channel recording.
Separate two questions. The configuration determines which cell membrane is accessible: an intact patch in cell-attached recording, an excised inside-out patch or outside-out patch, or intracellular access in whole-cell recording. The recording mode determines what is commanded and what is observed: voltage clamp commands an electric potential difference and measures electric current; current clamp commands electric current and measures membrane potential. Whole-cell recording supports both modes. A patch can contain several ion channels; a small recording area does not establish that only one is present.
The 1976 article Single-channel currents recorded from membrane of denervated frog muscle fibres describes an extracellular fire-polished pipette with a 3–5μm opening and 2–5MΩ electrical resistance. It contained saline and a channel-activating compound. Two separate intracellular electrodes supplied local voltage clamp of the muscle fibre; the patch amplifier measured local electric current. Cooling to 6–8∘C and hyperpolarization helped resolve elementary events. Figure 2 shows step-like pulses with a 200Hz filter at −120mV and 8∘C. Discrete amplitudes and overlapping events supported individual ion channel openings rather than a smoothly varying population response. This was neither whole-cell recording through the patch pipette nor current clamp. The specialized conditions improved visibility but limit generalization to warmer preparations; filtering can conceal brief openings.[ref]
For a new single-channel recording experiment, useful controls include a matched recording without the activating compound, controlled membrane potential, repeated seal tests, and an explicitly stated filter frequency response. These are proposed controls, not claims that every one was performed in that 1976 figure. Changing membrane potential tests the single-channel current-voltage relation; changing the recording filter tests whether a short pulse's apparent amplitude is an instrument artifact. A flat baseline establishes neither an absence of ion channels nor an absence of very brief events.

Patch pipette

Words: 41
Patch clamp OurBigBook.com
A patch pipette is the tapered glass, solution-filled probe used in patch clamp. Its electrode connects the solution to an amplifier, with another electrode referencing the bath. The open-tip electrical resistance differs from the much larger gigaohm seal electrical resistance. After break-in, a narrow or partly obstructed tip contributes to patch-clamp series resistance.

Gigaohm seal (Rseal​≳109Ω)

Words: 151 Articles: 1
Patch clamp OurBigBook.com
A gigaohm seal is the high electrical resistance contact between the glass rim and cell membrane, also called a gigaseal. It suppresses a bypass route around the membrane patch; it does not make the membrane patch itself impermeable. The 1981 methods used pulled, coated and heat-polished pipettes, a chlorided silver electrode and a pressure connection. Clean glass and suction supported tight seals; coating reduced pipette-to-bath capacitance and recording noise, rather than being required for sealing.[ref]

Seal leak current (Iseal​=Vp​/Rseal​)

Words: 76
Gigaohm seal OurBigBook.com
Seal leak current bypasses the membrane patch through an imperfect seal. For an ideal ohmic seal to a zero-voltage bath, Iseal​=Vp​/Rseal​, positive from pipette to bath. At ∣Vp​∣=50mV and Rseal​=1GΩ its magnitude is 50pA, far larger than the synthetic 0.8pA single-channel step. A stable baseline can be subtracted, but changing leakage can mimic a biological response. Intrinsic membrane leak through ion channels is distinct from this bypass: interpreting both as the same electrical conductance obscures whether the biological cell or the seal changed.

Cell-attached recording

Words: 53
Patch clamp OurBigBook.com
In cell-attached recording, the membrane under the patch pipette remains intact and the cytosol is retained. If bath voltage is zero, cell-interior voltage is Vcell​ and pipette voltage is Vp​, the patch's inside-minus-outside membrane potential is Vcell​−Vp​. Commanding Vp​ alone does not determine that difference when Vcell​ is unknown or changing. This is especially relevant to single-channel current-voltage relations.

Single-channel recording

Words: 126 Articles: 1
Patch clamp OurBigBook.com
Single-channel recording resolves individual ion channel opening events as changes in electric current. The distinction is resolution, not an absolute rule about configuration: rare, sufficiently large events can also be resolved during whole-cell recording. Simultaneously open identical ion channels can give successive current levels; indistinguishable amplitudes alone do not prove a unique channel identity.

Single-channel current-voltage relation (i=g(V−Erev​))

Words: 80
Single-channel recording OurBigBook.com
For an ideal open ion channel with constant electrical conductance g, membrane potential V and reversal potential Erev​, define outward electric current as positive:
i=g(V−Erev​).
(7)
This is an Ohm's law model of the open state, not a universal channel law or a rule for opening probability. In the synthetic figure, g=10pS and Erev​=0mV. Because 1pS⋅1mV=10−3pA, the open-state electric currents at −80 and −40mV are −0.8 and −0.4pA. Zero electric current at the reversal potential does not imply a closed ion channel. Real ion channels can have nonlinear responses, so the straight line is an explicit idealization.

Inside-out patch

Words: 32
Patch clamp OurBigBook.com
An inside-out patch is an excised membrane patch whose cytosol side faces the bath. Bath changes can therefore test effects on the intracellular face of an ion channel, with the extracellular face exposed to pipette solution.

Outside-out patch

Words: 36
Patch clamp OurBigBook.com
An outside-out patch is an excised membrane patch whose extracellular side faces the bath. It can form on withdrawal after whole-cell recording, with the intracellular face exposed to pipette solution. The orientation determines which side a bath-applied substance reaches.

Whole-cell recording

Words: 780 Articles: 6
Patch clamp OurBigBook.com
Whole-cell recording establishes intracellular electrical access by rupturing the membrane under a sealed patch pipette while retaining the gigaohm seal. Under adequate voltage clamp, the measured electric current combines contributions from accessible ion channels, membrane capacitance and seal leak current. Current clamp instead follows membrane potential while supplying a chosen electric current. Whole-cell recording is useful for linking a biological cell's total electrical response to its ion channels, but neither mode automatically controls distant dendrites or preserves the original cytosol.
In the 1981 methods demonstration, a bovine chromaffin biological cell was tested before and after patch rupture. Small voltage clamp steps produced a much larger capacitive transient after break-in. Integrating it gave 5pF for a 13μm cell; its decay indicated patch-clamp series resistance below 20MΩ. Depolarizing commands then revealed ionic electric currents. Separate current clamp recordings showed spontaneous action potentials. The comparison established access to the cell interior, rather than a claim that every pipette command equals membrane potential. Slower transients sometimes indicated incomplete rupture, and these small-cell results do not establish spatial control of a branched neuron.[ref]

Patch-clamp series resistance (Rs​)

Words: 195
Whole-cell recording OurBigBook.com
Patch-clamp series resistance, also called patch-clamp access resistance, is the effective electrical resistance between the pipette's sensed voltage and the cell interior. It includes tip access and any remaining obstruction after break-in. For injected electric current I into the biological cell, an ideal resistive access path gives
Vp​−V=IRs​.
(8)
Thus 1nA through 20MΩ produces a 20mV difference: a substantial possible voltage clamp error. The electric current in this equation is the access-path current, excluding any bypass seal leak current. In current clamp, the same access drop contaminates the pipette voltage during injection. Bridge compensation subtracts an estimated IRs​; an estimate that changes during recording leaves an error.
An independent passive voltage clamp calculation makes both speed and error visible. Write v=V−EL​ and vp​=Vp​−EL​, with fixed leak reversal potential EL​, constant membrane electrical resistance Rm​ and membrane capacitance Cm​. Assume an ideal command at the pipette node and omit seal leak current and pipette capacitance. Electric charge conservation gives
Cm​dtdv​=Rs​vp​−v​−Rm​v​.
(9)
For a step vp​=ΔV from v(0)=0, the ordinary differential equation gives
v(t)=ΔVRs​+Rm​Rm​​(1−e−t/τvc​),τvc​=Cm​Rs​+Rm​Rs​Rm​​.
(10)
With the figure's parameters and ΔV=10mV, the time constant is 0.909ms, the final membrane rise is 9.091mV, and access-path electric current falls from 500 to 45.45pA. Only when Rm​≫Rs​ does the time constant approach Rs​Cm​ and the final voltage approach the command. Actual voltage clamp also depends on amplifier feedback control and the space clamp problem.

Membrane capacitance (Cm​)

Words: 101 Articles: 1
Whole-cell recording OurBigBook.com
Membrane capacitance is the capacitance associated with separated electric charge across cell membrane. A local ideal capacitor has charging electric current IC​=Cm​dV/dt. If a known actual membrane voltage change is ΔV, integrating the charging transient after subtracting sustained ionic and leak components gives Cm​=ΔV−1∫IC​dt. Pipette capacitance, finite patch-clamp series resistance and imperfect transient subtraction can bias the estimate. A capacitive transient is not by itself an ion channel opening.
Membrane capacitive ion budget (Δc=Cm​AΔV/(zFV))
Words: 40
Membrane capacitance OurBigBook.com
When a single ion species supplies the net charging of a cell membrane, its bulk concentration increment is Δc=Cm​AΔV/(zFV). Opposing ionic Electric currents can make gross entry exceed this minimum net electric charge budget. A large membrane potential change can coexist with approximate bulk electroneutrality.

Space clamp

Words: 43
Whole-cell recording OurBigBook.com
The space clamp problem is the failure to maintain the commanded membrane potential throughout a spatially extended biological cell. A soma voltage clamp can coexist with substantial voltage changes in distant dendrites or an axon. Reducing patch-clamp series resistance improves access at the recording site, but does not eliminate electrical separation within the neuron.

Cytosol dialysis

Words: 199
Whole-cell recording OurBigBook.com
Cytosol dialysis is exchange between the cytosol and pipette solution through the opening used in conventional whole-cell recording. Diffusion can change ion concentrations and dilute soluble regulators of ion channels. A diminishing response can therefore reflect the recording's alteration of the biological cell, rather than the experimental treatment.
A direct motivating example is the 1988 article Muscarinic activation of ionic currents measured by a new whole-cell recording method. In rat lacrimal gland biological cells, the acetylcholine response in conventional whole-cell recording lasted about five minutes. With a pore-forming substance in the patch pipette instead of open break-in, the response remained undiminished after one hour. The readout was activation of calcium-activated potassium and Cl− ion electric currents; preserving the response supported a role for retained cytoplasmic components. The authors also tested the substance extracellularly and observed reversible increases in cation electrical conductance. This comparison motivates perforated patch recording, but does not show that every intracellular constituent or every ion channel response is preserved. [ref]
Practical controls are matched pipette and bath compositions, recording elapsed time after break-in, time-matched untreated preparations, and tracking both patch-clamp series resistance and baseline leakage. Comparing conventional whole-cell recording with perforated patch recording can separate loss of soluble components from an intended treatment effect, but only if electrical access is characterized in both. These are controls suggested by the mechanisms above, not a new set of measured results.

Perforated patch recording

Words: 47
Whole-cell recording OurBigBook.com
Perforated patch recording obtains intracellular electrical access through pores in the patch under the patch pipette, with less open exchange of large cytoplasmic components than conventional whole-cell recording. Pore selectivity matters: retaining some components does not guarantee unchanged ion concentrations. Monitor patch-clamp series resistance as access develops and distinguish a perforated patch from accidental full rupture.

Current clamp

Words: 306 Articles: 1
Patch clamp OurBigBook.com
Current clamp prescribes injected electric current while recording membrane potential. A constant command does not force membrane potential to remain constant: a neuron can produce action potentials or synaptic potentials while that command is unchanged. At zero commanded electric current, the amplifier still measures membrane potential; intrinsic ionic electric currents continue. The name concerns current supplied by the instrument, not the cancellation of all currents in the biological cell.
In whole-cell recording, the measured pipette voltage during a current pulse includes the patch-clamp series resistance drop. A modern authored methods article explicitly describes current-pulse protocols and this distortion.[ref] Check the access contribution with small pulses and distinguish the immediate pipette-voltage jump from the slower membrane capacitance response. A zero-input interval measures a baseline, not proof that the instrument has no voltage offset. The passive example below explains these distinctions without asserting any new physiological measurements.

Passive membrane response in current clamp (τm​=Rm​Cm​)

Words: 177
Current clamp OurBigBook.com
Model a spatially uniform cell membrane as a capacitor of membrane capacitance Cm​ in parallel with membrane electrical resistance Rm​ and a fixed leak reversal potential EL​. Exclude active ion channels, seal leak current and pipette capacitance. For electric current I injected into the biological cell, electric charge conservation yields
Cm​dtdV​=I−Rm​V−EL​​.
(11)
Starting at V(0)=EL​ and applying constant I gives the ordinary differential equation solution
V(t)=EL​+IRm​(1−e−t/τm​),τm​=Rm​Cm​.
(12)
The steady state rise is IRm​; the time constant is Rm​Cm​. With I=50pA, Rm​=200MΩ, Cm​=50pF and EL​=−70mV, the rise is 10mV and τm​=10ms. At one time constant the rise is 10(1−e−1)mV≈6.321mV. The figure's uncompensated pipette voltage adds IRs​=1mV for Rs​=20MΩ. The membrane voltage is continuous at step onset in this model, while the pipette voltage immediately acquires that access drop.
Checking the units is instructive: electrical resistance times capacitance has units ΩF=s, and electric current times electrical resistance has units of voltage. Unlike the passive voltage clamp transient under patch-clamp series resistance, this ideal current clamp membrane time constant is set by Rm​Cm​, not Rs​Cm​. Strong current steps can recruit voltage-gated ion channels; the passive model then fails and cannot generate an action potential. Small pulses of both signs, stable access and repeated baseline measurements help test whether the passive approximation is appropriate.

Computational neuroscience

Words: 3k Articles: 53
Neuroscience OurBigBook.com
Mathematical and computational models connect neural mechanisms, measured responses and proposed information-processing functions. Their predictions require comparison with experiments; matching observations does not uniquely identify the biological mechanism.

Path integration (θ˙=ω,p˙​=v(cosθ,sinθ)T)

Words: 42
Computational neuroscience OurBigBook.com
Updating an internal position or heading estimate from self-motion signals, such as angular velocity and translation. In an ideal planar case, θ˙=ω and p˙​=v(cosθ,sinθ)T. Integrating biased or noisy inputs accumulates errors, motivating correction by landmarks and other external cues.

Attractor network

Words: 79 Articles: 1
Computational neuroscience OurBigBook.com
A dynamical neural-network model whose activity tends toward stable states or sets. Recurrent excitation and inhibition can maintain a representation after the original input ends. The model must specify stability and noise consequences to predict behavior.

Bump attractor

Words: 43
Attractor network OurBigBook.com
A localized population-activity pattern in a network with a continuous family of possible represented positions. Noise can shift the pattern's center, producing drift in a remembered continuous variable while the pattern remains present. This yields testable relationships between delay activity and report errors.

Gabor filter

Words: 126
Computational neuroscience OurBigBook.com
A Gabor filter has a kernel formed by multiplying a Gaussian function by a sinusoid or a complex oscillation. In two-dimensional image processing, its orientation and spatial frequency select local image structure; evaluating the kernel's translated dot product with an image is spatial filtering. The real even example under signed spatial filter model of a simple cell uses a cosine.
There is experimental motivation for this family without making every simple cell an exact Gabor filter. Jones and Palmer fitted two-dimensional Gabor filters to measured spatial and spectral response profiles of simple cells in cat cortex and compared independently estimated parameters as a test of spatial linearity. Their reported residuals supported the approximation in that dataset. The chosen parameters and orientation tuning curve in this article are not extracted from their measurements. [ref]

Dynamic clamp

Words: 65
Computational neuroscience OurBigBook.com
A dynamic clamp measures a real neuron's voltage, updates a conductance model in real time and injects the resulting current, for example I=g(t)(E−V). It implements a virtual conductance without holding the voltage fixed. It can add artificial synapses, couple real neurons into a hybrid network or test how a voltage-dependent conductance affects excitability. Sampling delay and the injection site limit fidelity to spatially distributed biological channels.

Three-neuron ring stability ((1+τλ)3=Γ)

Words: 75
Computational neuroscience OurBigBook.com
For a directed three-neuron rate ring τx˙i​=−xi​+Wi,i−1​tanh(βxi−1​), the linearization has characteristic equation (1+τλ)3=Γ, where Γ=β3W13​W32​W21​. Positive loop gain has strict linear asymptotic stability for Γ<1. Negative loop gain has it for −8<Γ<0; at Γ=−8 a complex pair crosses the imaginary axis at frequency 3​/τ. The saturating cubic gives a supercritical Hopf bifurcation under an ordinary loop-gain variation. This directed system does not inherit the energy-descent property of a symmetric Hopfield network.

Leaky integrate-and-fire model (CV˙=−gL​(V−EL​)+I(t))

Words: 488 Articles: 1
Computational neuroscience OurBigBook.com
The leaky integrate-and-fire model combines a passive equation for membrane potential with a firing rule. Between events, inward-positive applied electric current I(t) obeys
CdtdV​=−gL​(V−EL​)+I(t),R=gL​1​,τ=gL​C​=RC,
(13)
where C>0 is membrane capacitance, gL​>0 is the leak conductance, R is the corresponding electrical resistance, and EL​ is the leak reversal potential. Here the leak conductance is constant. The time constant τ describes passive relaxation. When V first reaches a threshold Vθ​ from below, record an action potential event and reset V to Vr​<Vθ​. In the version used here, hold V=Vr​ for a fixed neuronal refractory period tref​, then resume integration. See 1.3 Integrate-And-Fire Models.
For constant I, with t=0 at the start of an integration interval and V(0)=Vinitial​, the exact subthreshold solution is
V(t)=EL​+RI+(Vinitial​−EL​−RI)e−t/τ.
(14)
The equilibrium point of this passive equation is V∞​=EL​+RI. Subtracting V∞​ leaves d(V−V∞​)/dt=−(V−V∞​)/τ, explaining the exponential function. This solution applies only until a threshold event or a change in I. Starting below threshold, constant input produces repeated events if V∞​>Vθ​; if V∞​=Vθ​, the threshold is approached asymptotically and never reached at finite time.
For a worked example, choose
EL​=Vr​=Vinitial​=−65mV,Vθ​=−50mV,τ=20ms,R=100MΩ,tref​=2ms.
(15)
These imply gL​=10nS and C=200pF. All these parameters are illustrative model choices, not measurements from a particular neuron. With I=200pA, Ohm's law gives RI=20mV and hence V∞​=−45mV. Thus
V(t)=−45mV−20mVe−t/(20ms).
(16)
At threshold, e−t/τ=1/4, so the first event occurs after T=20ln4ms≈27.7259ms. Each subsequent cycle includes the 2ms neuronal refractory period, giving
f=T+tref​1​≈33.6407Hz.
(17)
This is the ideal sustained firing rate; the first-event latency is T, not T+tref​.
With I=100pA instead, RI=10mV and V∞​=−55mV. From the same initial state, V(t)=−55mV−10mVe−t/τ stays below −50mV: no events occur, however long this current is held. The critical sustained current is (Vθ​−EL​)/R=150pA; equality gives asymptotic approach rather than finite-time firing.
The leak gives old inputs progressively less influence, while capacitance prevents an ordinary finite electric current step from changing V instantly. This combination makes the leaky integrate-and-fire model useful for exploring input summation, event timing and network activity at low computational cost. Its fixed parameters and reset omit the evolving voltage-gated ion channels of the Hodgkin-Huxley model, spatial integration in dendrites and mechanisms of neural adaptation. Treating a synapse as a prescribed I(t) also omits its voltage-dependent driving force unless a conductance term is added. See 1.4 Limitations of the Leaky Integrate-and-Fire Model and constant-input firing rate of a leaky integrate-and-fire neuron.

Constant-input firing rate of a leaky integrate-and-fire neuron

Words: 56
Leaky integrate-and-fire model OurBigBook.com
For Cm​V˙=−gL​(V−VL​)+I, reset V0​<Vθ​ and no explicit refractory interval, define Ic​=gL​(Vθ​−VL​) and τm​=Cm​/gL​. Constant current gives
r(I)={0,[τm​log((I−gL​(V0​−VL​))/(I−Ic​))]−1,​I≤Ic​,I>Ic​.​
(18)
The threshold is approached only asymptotically at I=Ic​. At large current, r∼I/[Cm​(Vθ​−V0​)]. Adding an absolute neuronal refractory period changes the denominator to T(I)+tref​ and makes the firing rate saturate rather than grow without bound.

Hodgkin-Huxley model

Words: 397 Articles: 2
Computational neuroscience OurBigBook.com
A conductance-based Hodgkin-Huxley model couples membrane potential to voltage-dependent channel-gating variables. It explains generation of action potentials through regenerative and opposing ionic electric currents, while its parameters and channel assumptions determine its biological domain of validity.
In the classical model, m describes sodium activation, h describes availability against sodium inactivation, and n describes potassium activation. Each follows two-state ion-channel gating, with its own voltage-dependent rates. The available electrical conductances are
gNa​=gˉ​Na​m3h,gK​=gˉ​K​n4.
(19)
The barred quantities are maximum electrical conductances. The factors have the interpretation of independent permissive gates in an ion channel: three activation factors and a distinct inactivation-availability factor for sodium, and four identical activation factors for potassium. Large h means availability; small h means inactivation. These are model assumptions, not a literal structural description of every ion channel. See Gerstner, Kistler, Naud and Paninski, Neuronal Dynamics (2014), §2.2: model definition and stochastic opening.
With inward-positive electric current, a single-compartment form is
CdtdV​=Iext​+gNa​(ENa​−V)+gK​(EK​−V)+gL​(EL​−V).
(20)
Here C is membrane capacitance, Iext​ is imposed inward electric current, gL​ is leak electrical conductance, and each E is a reversal potential. Use consistent units, and either whole-compartment quantities throughout or quantities per membrane area throughout. Opening changes electrical conductance; the reversal potential and present membrane potential determine the associated electric current. Coupling this equation to the voltage-dependent gates makes a generally nonlinear system of ordinary differential equations; a gate's fixed-voltage limit alone does not specify its evolving state during an action potential.
The original quantitative account is [ref]. The contrast with the leaky integrate-and-fire model is useful: here an action potential emerges from evolving ionic electric currents, whereas the simpler model records a threshold event and imposes a reset.

Planar reduction of the Hodgkin-Huxley model

Words: 131 Articles: 1
Hodgkin-Huxley model OurBigBook.com
Replacing the fast activation gate by m=m∞​(V), taking τn​(V)=τh​(V) and assuming n∞​(V)+h∞​(V)=K constant reduces the Hodgkin-Huxley model to equations for V,n when n(0)+h(0)=K. Indeed q=n+h satisfies τ(V)q˙​=K−q, so q=K and h=K−n. The FitzHugh-Nagumo model additionally simplifies the two resulting response functions to a cubic activation equation and a linear recovery equation.
Folded conductance-model nullcline
Words: 79
Planar reduction of the Hodgkin-Huxley model OurBigBook.com
For g(v,n)=γK​(v+vK​)n4−(1−v)(H−n)M(v), with rapidly increasing saturating activation M, the zero-current nullcline satisfies n4/(H−n)=(1−v)M(v)/[γK​(v+vK​)] in the physical strip. The left side increases strictly, so it defines one height for each voltage. Since gn​>0, its slope is −gv​/gn​. Rapid activation can make gv​ negative between two positive-slope current regimes, giving two descending attracting branches and an ascending repelling branch in the voltage–recovery phase plane. Sufficient activation steepness is a parameter condition; the shape is not forced by monotonicity alone.

Mutually excitatory saturating rate network (τx˙=−x+g(y),g(z)=ma2z2/(σ2+a2z2))

Words: 72
Computational neuroscience OurBigBook.com
The symmetric two-neuron rate model has nonnegative activity and saturating recurrent input. Every equilibrium has x=y: otherwise monotonicity of g gives a contradiction. With positive parameters it has three distinct equilibria exactly when am>2σ, namely zero and z±​=(m±m2−4σ2/a2​)/2. The lower positive equilibrium is a saddle and the origin and upper equilibrium are stable nodes. The resulting two attracting activity levels model a persistent switch rather than a spiking waveform.

Linear-nonlinear-Poisson cascade model (r(t)=g(b+(k∗s)(t)))

Words: 98 Articles: 1
Computational neuroscience OurBigBook.com
A stimulus passes through a linear temporal or spatial filter, then a nonnegative nonlinear rate function. A conditionally Inhomogeneous Poisson process generates spikes at that rate. The filter and nonlinearity can be fitted from data and tested on held-out trials. Refractoriness and spike-history correlations require extensions beyond this basic cascade.

Poisson spike-train likelihood fitting (ℓ=∑i​logλ(ti​)−∫λ(t)dt)

Words: 51
Linear-nonlinear-Poisson cascade model OurBigBook.com
For a stimulus-conditioned Inhomogeneous Poisson process, the event log-likelihood is the displayed expression. A causal filter expansion λ(t)=exp[b+∑a​wa​(s∗ba​)(t)] can be fitted by maximum likelihood estimation, with a smoothness or size penalty and held-out validation. The integral term penalizes predicted spikes that did not occur; fitting only stimulus values at observed spikes omits this essential part.

Spike-triggered average (k(u)=K−1∑i​s(ti​−u))

Words: 120 Articles: 1
Computational neuroscience OurBigBook.com
Average the stimulus history preceding each observed spike, after removing the stimulus mean. With white Gaussian stimulation and a suitable one-filter encoding model, the result is proportional to the relevant linear filter. An even nonlinearity can make the average vanish despite strong stimulus dependence, so averaging alone is not universally sufficient.

Stimulus-correlated spike-triggered averaging

Words: 69
Spike-triggered average OurBigBook.com
For a single linear filter followed by a rate nonlinearity and a Gaussian stimulus-history vector s with covariance C, Gaussian integration by parts gives E[sg(kTs)]∝Ck. Thus a spike-triggered average estimates Ck, rather than k directly, when the stimulus is correlated. Covariance correction, with regularization if necessary, can recover the filter direction. For an even nonlinearity the proportionality factor can vanish; then a one-filter average is insufficient.

Neural coding

Words: 1k Articles: 36
Computational neuroscience OurBigBook.com
How neural responses represent variables relevant to an organism. A coding claim specifies both which response features carry information and how a downstream system can use them.

Mixed selectivity

Words: 34
Neural coding OurBigBook.com
Dependence of a neural response on combinations of task variables. A cell can carry information about an object in a context and at a sequence position rather than encode only one of these variables.

Spike count (N)

Words: 25
Neural coding OurBigBook.com
The number of recorded action potentials in a specified interval. A count is a nonnegative integer; a fitted firing rate or an expected count need not be an integer.

Firing rate (r)

Words: 30
Neural coding OurBigBook.com
The number of action potentials per unit time, interpreted as an average over a stated window or as an intensity estimated from a spike train. Window size changes which temporal information remains visible.

Cell assembly

Words: 90 Articles: 1
Neural coding OurBigBook.com
A group of neurons whose coordinated activity and learned interactions can represent or participate in an experience. An assembly can overlap with assemblies for other events; it need not assign one private neuron to each memory.
Symmetric coactivity weights do not distinguish reversed episodes
Words: 56
Cell assembly OurBigBook.com
Suppose storing activities a1​,…,aT​ changes a matrix by ΔW=η∑t=1T​at​atT​. Any permutation of the activities leaves this sum unchanged. Therefore the update alone cannot distinguish an episode from its reversal. This is a restriction on the stated order-insensitive update, not on all Hebbian learning: trace learning, an evolving context or directed transitions can introduce order information.

Representational hierarchy theory

Words: 42
Neural coding OurBigBook.com
An account of regional specialization in terms of the complexity and conjunctions represented, rather than a strict division between perception and memory. The feature-conjunction account of perirhinal cortex proposes object-level combinations that resolve shared-feature ambiguity; higher-order relations can require further interactions.[ref]

Time cell

Words: 38
Neural coding OurBigBook.com
A neuron active preferentially at a particular part of a temporally extended task or interval. Temporal selectivity can coexist with selectivity for location, behavior and sequence identity; it is not a claim that the cell is an isolated clock.

Cognitive map

Words: 41
Neural coding OurBigBook.com
A representation of relations among locations or task states that can support inference beyond memorized stimulus–response pairs. The represented space need not be physically spatial. A cognitive-map hypothesis specifies which states and relations are encoded and what behaviour can use them.

Sharp-wave ripple

Words: 53
Neural coding OurBigBook.com
A hippocampal population event involving a sharp wave and fast ripple oscillation, often associated with internally generated ensemble activity. Selective interruption can test its contribution to memory, but disrupting an event does not by itself identify the content or computational role of each participating sequence.[ref]

Allocentric spatial representation

Words: 49
Neural coding OurBigBook.com
A representation of position or orientation in an external reference frame. Transforming a retinal direction to a world location generally needs eye position, head orientation, self-location and depth or scene geometry. A label in world coordinates is a description of the code, not an explanation of how it develops.

Spatial view cell

Words: 45
Neural coding OurBigBook.com
A neuron selective for a viewed location in external space. In the primate recordings motivating the term, eye-position and locomotion measurements distinguished the looked-at part of the environment from the animal’s self-location and head direction.[ref]

Place cell

Words: 69 Articles: 1
Neural coding OurBigBook.com
A neuron whose activity is spatially selective for the animal’s own location under specified conditions. Its field can depend on environment, task and sensory context; a visual view and self-location must be disentangled experimentally.
Hippocampal remapping
Words: 36
Place cell OurBigBook.com
A change in a hippocampal spatial representation across environments or contexts. Models distinguish changes in firing rates, field locations and the relationships among simultaneously recorded units; visual cue changes need not produce one universal kind of response.

Head direction cell

Words: 43
Neural coding OurBigBook.com
A neuron whose firing varies with the orientation of the head relative to the environment. Preferred direction must be distinguished from gaze direction and self-location. Landmark rotation and cue-removal experiments test the visual anchor of this code.[ref]

Neural oscillation

Words: 107 Articles: 3
Neural coding OurBigBook.com
Rhythmic variation in neural signals. Frequency-band averages can obscure brief events; the timing and duration of bursts can matter independently of mean spectral power.
Theta oscillation
Words: 40
Neural oscillation OurBigBook.com
A neural rhythm in the frequency range conventionally called theta. In rodent hippocampal experiments it provides a temporal reference for comparing the firing of local and remote cells. A matching rhythm does not alone identify the direction or necessity of communication.
Beta oscillation
Words: 25
Neural oscillation OurBigBook.com
A neural oscillation in the frequency band conventionally termed beta, below gamma. Its functional interpretation depends on task, site and temporal structure rather than on frequency alone.
Gamma oscillation
Words: 18
Neural oscillation OurBigBook.com
A neural oscillation in a relatively high-frequency band conventionally termed gamma. Exact band boundaries vary by study and recording method.

Local field potential

Words: 36
Neural coding OurBigBook.com
An extracellular voltage reflecting weighted contributions from nearby and sometimes more distant neuronal currents. Its spatial sensitivity depends on anatomy, electrode placement and signal properties; it is not simply the firing rate of the nearest cell.

Neural decoding

Words: 35
Neural coding OurBigBook.com
Inferring a stimulus, task state or behavior from neural measurements. Successful decoding demonstrates information accessible to the chosen decoder; it does not by itself establish the neural site's causal necessity, exclusive representation or downstream use.

Population coding

Words: 249 Articles: 5
Neural coding OurBigBook.com
Representation through the joint activity of multiple neurons. Information can reside in relative activity patterns even when the overall mean activity changes little. Neural decoding tests whether recorded patterns carry accessible information under a specified analysis.
Noise correlation
Words: 37
Population coding OurBigBook.com
Statistical dependence between neural responses remaining after the modeled task-related mean has been removed. Residual dependence can reflect shared state or omitted task variables as well as biological noise, so its interpretation depends on the conditioning model.
Neural population state space
Words: 178 Articles: 3
Population coding OurBigBook.com
Coordinates describing the joint activity of a neural population, often using one coordinate per cell or fitted latent variable. A trajectory connects states over time. A useful reduced description requires evidence that it retains the neural and behavioral properties relevant to the intended claim.
Linear latent coordinates are not unique without constraints
Words: 65
Neural population state space OurBigBook.com
In the observation model y=Cz+b, let Q be an orthogonal matrix. Replacing z by Qz and C by CQT leaves y unchanged because QTQ=I. Thus reconstruction alone does not give each latent axis a unique biological meaning. A particular stochastic model can restrict this symmetry through its prior and parameter constraints; the algebra does not claim every fitted latent model has every rotational ambiguity.
Neural manifold
Words: 38
Neural population state space OurBigBook.com
A proposed lower-dimensional set around which recorded population states are organized. The estimated dimension depends on sampling, noise, preprocessing and the scale of variation. A visually smooth embedding is not by itself proof of an intrinsic biological manifold.
Neural trajectory
Words: 31
Neural population state space OurBigBook.com
The evolution of a population representation over time. A trajectory estimated after trial averaging or strong smoothing can differ from every individual-trial trajectory; this distinction matters for claims about neural dynamics.

Persistent neural activity

Words: 29
Neural coding OurBigBook.com
Sustained neural activity outlasting a triggering input. Recurrent network dynamics can support persistent representations, but a sustained average signal can also conceal temporally variable events across trials or cells.

Receptive field

Words: 196 Articles: 2
Neural coding OurBigBook.com
The region and stimulus features whose variation influences a sensory neuron's response. A visual receptive field may include spatially distinct ON and OFF regions; a linear receptive-field kernel is a signed weighting map, while the full response can be nonlinear and depend on stimulus history.
ON and OFF receptive-field subregions
Words: 86
Receptive field OurBigBook.com
ON and OFF receptive-field subregions distinguish locations by response polarity. In the classic mapping experiment, a bright spot in an ON region increased firing during illumination; illumination in an OFF region suppressed maintained firing and/or evoked a discharge when the light disappeared. If maintained firing was very low, suppression could be hard to see. The recorded decrease alone did not distinguish direct inhibition at a synapse from reduced excitation. [ref] These are functional regions in visual space, not compartments of a cell body.
Visual contrast (C=(L−L0​)/L0​)
Words: 65
Receptive field OurBigBook.com
For the toy models here, visual contrast means brightness relative to a positive uniform background L0​: C(x,y)=(L(x,y)−L0​)/L0​. Positive values mean brighter than background, negative values darker, and zero unchanged. This convention separates spatial structure from the background level. A sinusoid C=acos(⋯) with 0≤a≤1 keeps L=L0​(1+C) nonnegative. Different experimental conventions for visual contrast require their own definitions; the toy values below do not specify a historical stimulus intensity.

Temporal coding

Words: 69 Articles: 1
Neural coding OurBigBook.com
Representation by spike timing, latency, phase or relative timing across neurons, beyond a chosen count summary. Its interpretation requires a timing reference and a decoder capable of resolving the relevant precision.
Neural phase locking
Words: 38
Temporal coding OurBigBook.com
A tendency for neural spikes to occur at preferred phases of a periodic stimulus. It supplies timing information without requiring one spike on every cycle. Its precision and usable frequency range depend on the cell population and conditions.

Rate coding

Words: 31
Neural coding OurBigBook.com
Representation by a neuron's firing frequency or the expected spike count in a chosen time window. The window length and averaging convention matter; equal counts do not imply equal temporal patterns.

Spike train (n(t)=∑i​δ(t−ti​))

Words: 106 Articles: 2
Neural coding OurBigBook.com
A sequence of action potential times, represented mathematically as a point process or a sum of Dirac deltas. Its event counts, intervals and correlations summarize different aspects of neural activity.
Interspike interval (Si​=ti+1​−ti​)
Words: 27
Spike train OurBigBook.com
An interspike interval is the elapsed time between consecutive action potentials in a spike train. Its probability distribution and dependence on previous activity can reveal a neuronal refractory period even when the average firing rate is unchanged.
Time-rescaled spike-train diagnostics (zi​=∫ti​ti+1​​λ(t∣Ht​)dt)
Words: 52
Spike train OurBigBook.com
For a correctly specified conditional rate, transformed interspike intervals have independent unit-exponential distributions, apart from observation-boundary censoring. Their transforms 1−e−zi​ should be uniform. Distributional checks and serial-correlation checks assess a fitted spike model on held-out data. A history-dependent model must include past spikes in its conditional rate; stimulus-only Poisson spike-train likelihood fitting cannot automatically capture refractoriness.
